proposals.title: Soil-Moisture Probe Lag Compensation for Apple Orchard Irrigation Control
proposals.markdown:
## Soil-Moisture Probe Lag Compensation for Apple Orchard Irrigation Control

**Company:** Described problem works in agriculture. [C999] Challenge C999-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Nenad Ilić is an Associate Professor in the Department of Field and Vegetable Crops, Faculty of Agriculture. [R0662]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
After rainfall the apple orchard irrigation controllers overwater because soil moisture probes react slowly, and a fixed pause after rainfall did not solve the problem (C999-CH1). [C999-CH1] A fixed pause inserted after rainfall did not solve the overwatering problem and young trees now show root stress (C999-CH1). [C999-CH1] The orchard covers 60 hectares and the company holds three seasons of probe readings, weather station data and yield records (C999-CH1). [C999-CH1]

### Prior work
- A 2018 study reports a dynamic neural network trained on past soil moisture, precipitation, and climatic measurements that predicts volumetric water content one day ahead with an R 2 value above 0.94 across three field sites, and achieves water savings of 20–46% compared with a rule-based threshold irrigation system. [W2896715775]
- A 2019 study reports an irrigation scheduling approach using capacitance probes for real-time soil water monitoring in a nectarine orchard, deriving irrigation factors from measured soil water deficits across the full growing season. [W2924508481]

### Research questions
1. Can a data-driven model trained on the three-season probe and weather archive predict post-rainfall volumetric water content at the probe depth accurately enough to replace the raw probe reading in the irrigation decision logic? Measured as RMSE and R² of predicted versus measured soil moisture on a held-out season, with a target R² above 0.90.
2. Does replacing the raw probe signal with the model's predicted moisture value reduce false irrigation events after rainfall compared with the current controller, without increasing root-stress indicators? Measured as the count of irrigation triggers within 24 hours of a rainfall event ≥5 mm, and soil moisture exceedance above field capacity, across the validation season.

### Approach
- Characterise the probe lag: use the three-season archive to quantify the time and magnitude of the gap between the probe reading and the weather-station-derived estimate of post-rain soil water content at each depth, applying the capacitive sensor calibration methods from the researcher's published work on multi-depth probe arrays.
- Build a predictive moisture model: train a dynamic model (feeding past probe readings, rainfall, temperature and ET₀ computed via Penman–Monteith) on two seasons of archive data to predict actual volumetric water content one step ahead, bypassing the lag period after rain.
- Develop a lag-aware decision rule: embed the model output into the irrigation feedback logic following the sensor-based decision framework the researcher published for precision irrigation, replacing the fixed-pause heuristic with a model-gated trigger that withholds irrigation when predicted moisture exceeds the target threshold.
- Validate in the field: run the new controller logic in parallel with the existing system during one growing season, logging both decisions and comparing false-trigger rates and soil moisture exceedance against the baseline.

### Plan

| Period | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 1–3 | Propose that a master's student be recruited to the project to transfer and clean the three-season archive, document probe placement and soil type at each monitoring point, and run the sensor calibration procedure for the orchard soil, supervised by Nenad Ilić and a nominated company contact. The researcher provides calibration protocols from published work on multi-depth probe arrays. | A labelled, calibrated dataset covering three seasons; a characterisation report quantifying probe lag by rainfall intensity band and soil depth. |
| Months 4–6 | The master's student trains and cross-validates a dynamic predictive model on two seasons of the archive, testing both the lag profile and the model's post-rain prediction on the held-out season. The researcher reviews model outputs against the decision-framework logic. A revised controller rule set is drafted and reviewed with the company engineer. | A validated predictive model (R² target ≥ 0.90 on the held-out season); a draft lag-aware decision rule; a project paper submitted to a peer-reviewed journal. |
| Months 7–9 | The lag-aware controller rule is deployed in a shadow mode alongside the live system during the irrigation season. The company engineer logs both the old and new trigger decisions daily; the master's student compares false-trigger counts and soil moisture exceedance against the three-season baseline. | A field-trial report comparing false irrigation event rates and soil moisture exceedance; a go/no-go recommendation for full deployment. |
| Months 10–12 | If the trial is positive, the researcher and the company engineer integrate the model into the production controller and document the updated system. Remaining calibration edge cases (heavy rainfall, irrigation overlap) are resolved. Final reporting to the EINSTEIN programme. | A production-ready lag-compensation module for the orchard controller; final project report; journal paper revision submitted. |

### First six months
- Month 1 — Data transfer and audit: the company exports all three seasons of probe readings, weather station logs and yield records to the researcher's group; the master's student documents sensor placement, depths and soil type at each of the 60-ha monitoring points.
- Month 2 — Calibration: applying the researcher's multi-depth capacitive probe calibration protocol to the orchard soil type; the master's student and the company engineer take reference soil samples at representative orchard blocks to anchor the calibration.
- Month 3 — Lag characterisation: the master's student quantifies the post-rainfall probe lag (time to equilibration, magnitude by rainfall intensity band and depth) across the three-season archive; Nenad Ilić reviews outputs.
- Months 4–6 — Model development: the master's student trains the dynamic predictive moisture model on two seasons, validates it on the third, and drafts the lag-aware decision rule; the researcher and the company engineer review the rule against operational constraints before the irrigation season begins.

### What each side brings
- **Company:** Three seasons of soil moisture probe readings, weather station data and yield records from 60 hectares of apple orchards. [C999-CH1]
- **Faculty:** Nenad Ilić co-authored published work on capacitive soil moisture sensor calibration across soil types and long-term field stability of a multi-depth probe array. [SYN-PUB-07491, SYN-PUB-07495] Nenad Ilić holds a granted patent for a capacitive soil moisture probe with a multi-depth sensing array. [SYN-PAT-001] Nenad Ilić co-authored a sensor-based feedback decision framework for precision irrigation applicable to Pannonian Plain agro-ecological conditions. [SYN-PUB-07499] Nenad Ilić co-authored work on IoT cloud-based architectures with wireless sensor networks and MQTT messaging for irrigation scheduling, and led WATERWISE delivering mobile irrigation decision support across 20 farms. [SYN-PUB-07493, SYN-PUB-07496, SYN-PRJ-0003]

### Why this pair
The company has a well-defined sensor-lag problem and three seasons of data to solve it, but needs the calibration and decision-framework methods to turn that data into a working controller fix. Nenad Ilić brings exactly those methods: published capacitive probe calibration, a multi-depth probe patent, and a sensor-based irrigation decision framework. Neither side could do this alone: the company holds the orchard data and the live controller, while the researcher brings the calibration protocols and the decision logic that the model output must plug into.

- The company's orchard controllers overwater after rain because soil moisture probes react slowly, and the company holds three seasons of probe readings, weather station data and yield records from 60 hectares. [C999-CH1]
- Nenad Ilić co-authored work on capacitive soil moisture sensor calibration across soil types and on a sensor-based feedback decision framework for precision irrigation. [SYN-PUB-07491, SYN-PUB-07499]
- Nenad Ilić led WATERWISE as principal investigator, an applied project delivering irrigation decision support piloted across 20 farms. [SYN-PRJ-0003]

### Risks and constraints
- The published calibration work covers five Vojvodina soil types in irrigated maize and sunflower plots, and long-term stability in a chernozem profile under irrigated sugar beet and winter wheat. [SYN-PUB-07491, SYN-PUB-07495]
- The decision framework record covers field crops in Vojvodina (SYN-PUB-07499), and other irrigation records cover vegetables and sunflower (SYN-PUB-07492, SYN-PUB-07498); none of these records covers perennial tree crops or apple-specific root stress physiology. [SYN-PUB-07499, SYN-PUB-07492, SYN-PUB-07498]

### Agreed up front (proposed)
- Publication: the company reviews any manuscript for 45 days before submission; results describing proprietary field layouts or yield data may be anonymised at the company's request.
- Ownership: the lag-compensation model and any adapted decision rules belong to the company for use in its own orchards; the Faculty retains the underlying calibration methods and may reuse them in future research.
- Data access: the company transfers the three-season archive to the researcher's group under a signed data-sharing agreement before Month 1 begins; data is used only for this project and deleted from the Faculty's servers at project close.
- Preconditions: the data-sharing agreement and a joint project contract defining cost sharing and the company engineer's time commitment (minimum one day per week) are signed before work starts.

### Sources
- C999: Described problem
- C999-CH1: Our irrigation controllers in apple orchards overwater after rain because the soil moisture probes react slowly.
- R0662: Nenad Ilić
- SYN-PAT-001: Capacitive soil moisture probe with a multi-depth sensing array (2021)
- SYN-PRJ-0003: WATERWISE: irrigation advice for smallholders (2021)
- SYN-PUB-07491: Low-cost capacitive soil moisture probes: calibration across soil types (2021)
- SYN-PUB-07492: Deficit irrigation of vegetables in a changing climate (2020)
- SYN-PUB-07493: A smartphone-based decision support application for real-time irrigation scheduling in smallholder vegetable production (2022)
- SYN-PUB-07495: Calibration and long-term stability of a multi-depth capacitive soil moisture probe array under field conditions (2023)
- SYN-PUB-07496: Towards IoT-enabled irrigation management: integration of wireless soil moisture sensor networks with cloud-based dec... (2024)
- SYN-PUB-07498: Effects of regulated deficit irrigation at critical growth stages on sunflower yield and oil content in semi-arid con... (2020)
- SYN-PUB-07499: Precision irrigation in field crops: a review of sensor-based feedback systems and decision support frameworks applic... (2023)
- W2896715775: Dynamic Neural Network Modelling of Soil Moisture Content for Predictive Irrigation Scheduling (2018) https://openalex.org/W2896715775
- W2924508481: Irrigation Factor Approach Based on Soil Water Content: A Nectarine Orchard Case Study (2019) https://openalex.org/W2924508481
